body.estimand_functional: \((p,G)\longmapsto\mathsf{Cov}_p(G)\setminus\mathsf H_{\mathrm{soft}}(G)\), with \(\mathsf{Cov}_p\) evaluated chamberwise through \(\mathcal E_p\) and \(\mathsf H_{\mathrm{soft}}\) evaluated by the terminal actual-row certificates.

sampling_model.design: Population identification from one baseline and one unknown-target single-node soft-intervention context per latent node under noninjective mixing \(2\le p<q\).
sampling_model.units: Inputs are aligned population factorization data \(\mathcal R\) and the \(q+1\) population covariance matrices \(\{\Sigma^{(k)}\}_{k\in K}\); there is no finite-sample claim.
sampling_model.treatment: Each non-source context changes every incoming coefficient of one unknown latent target and retains every such edge. Targets are identified only up to one common latent permutation.
sampling_model.overlap: No treatment-overlap condition applies. Baseline and intervention variances are positive and may coincide. Covariance theorems use only declared finite generic loci, including \(\prod_{k\in V}(t_k-v_k)\ne0\), cover both adjacent sign chambers, and make no pointwise claim on neutral hyperplanes.
sampling_model.nuisance_estimation: Aligned factor directions and source laws modulo common permutation and diagonal scaling are population inputs. Recovery from raw laws and finite-sample tensor estimation are outside scope.

Problem 5.2 asks whether the higher-cumulant-compatible graph class is strictly contained in the covariance-compatible graph class.
The generic-soft covariance analysis and perfect-intervention graph-recovery clause are stated for injective mixing \(p\ge q\).
The paper treats unpaired observational and interventional data under generalized faithfulness and recovers an equivalence class.
Theorem 2.8 characterizes generic covariance-submatrix rank by trek separation.
The half-trek criterion supplies a polynomial-time sufficient certificate for generic rational identifiability.
The paper studies half-trek criteria for identifiability of latent-variable models.
Sections IV--V provide semidefinite tests and positive-semidefinite decomposition and realization machinery for latent causal structures.

In arXiv:2410.23102v1, Theorem 3.10 transfers a semialgebraic image through an affine-birational parametrization with positive localizing denominators, and Theorem 3.11 identifies its saturated vanishing ideal.

The paper uses tree dynamic programming over the primal graph of variables co-occurring in atomic constraints to accelerate existential Fourier--Motzkin elimination and cylindrical algebraic decomposition.

body.tldr: For noninjective soft-intervention linear causal disentanglement, \(2\le p<q\), covariance compatibility is a finite union of positive-real factor-line projections rather than an injective recovery problem. The information-frontier headline is a graph-specific compiler deciding whether a same-closure candidate lies generically in \(\mathsf{Cov}_p(G)\setminus\mathsf H_{\mathrm{soft}}(G)\), returning a positive realization cover or full-dimensional separator without unrestricted real quantifier elimination. This robust generic-chamber refinement is motivated by Problem 5.2, lies definitionally inside the matched-existential class \(\mathsf{soft2M}_{2,p}(G)\), and is not identified with the published covariance-compatible class. The mandatory first result completely classifies all eight branches of a \(p=2,q=4\) fork; the next proves the compiler on bounded covariance-terminal width with an explicit bit bound. Independently, compatibility is certified from the actual rows \(h_k^{\mathsf T}=\delta_k^{\mathsf T}(I_q-\Lambda^{(0)})^{-1}\) by terminal-copy linkage and affine support tests, and an explicit four-node minor refutes the generic-rank substitution in Theorem 3.15. Variance-neutral points remain in the ambient model: \(\prod_k(t_k-v_k)\ne0\) occurs only in theorem-specific covariance loci, and excluded hyperplanes receive no pointwise claim.

project_justification.gap: Problem 5.2 of Leyes Carreno, Meroni, and Seigal asks whether its covariance-compatible and higher-cumulant-compatible graph classes differ, but its overcomplete example proves parameter nonuniqueness rather than a graph-specific positive-real frontier. The robust class \(\mathsf{Cov}_p(G)\) refines the genericity requirement chamber by chamber, is definitionally contained in \(\mathsf{soft2M}_{2,p}(G)\), and is not identified with the published covariance-compatible class. Existing positive-semidefinite compatibility, affine-birational constraint transfer, half-trek criteria, equivalence-class recovery from unpaired interventions, and treewidth-accelerated general quantifier elimination do not decide the coupled noninjective branch union with the required realization-or-separator output. In the same paper, Equation (20) correctly derives compatibility from actual intervention rows, but the proof of Theorem 3.15 reaches the baseline-path class in Definition 3.14 by a nongeneric identification of independent change and baseline variables.
project_justification.niche: When \(p<q\), each rank-two covariance difference supplies two possible loading lines, while all contexts share one positive baseline decomposition and one candidate structural inverse. This finite nonconvex union must be decided chamber by chamber. Covariance-terminal width gives a graph-controlled route between one solved fork and the unrestricted problem.
project_justification.fill: The paper first proves the complete eight-branch \(p=2,q=4\) classification, then a realization-or-separator compiler for bounded covariance-terminal width with explicit certificate and bit complexity, and finally poses the all-graph compiler as the sole open information-frontier question. A separate terminal-copy theorem gives the corrected actual-row compatibility test, and a four-node counterexample identifies the precise invalid specialization in Theorem 3.15.

body.related_work: Leyes Carreno, Meroni, and Seigal (2025) derive the actual intervention-row system in Equation (20), define the baseline inverse-path class in Definition 3.14, and in the proof of Theorem 3.15 replace each independent change \(\lambda^{(k)}_{ki}-\lambda^{(0)}_{ki}\) by the baseline coefficient \(\lambda^{(0)}_{ki}\) while claiming generic rank is unchanged. Theorem 1.7 uses Theorem 3.15 to state recovery of that soft-compatible class, and Problems 5.1--5.2 ask for a combinatorial description and whether covariance enlarges the compatible DAG set. The terminal-copy theorem repairs the transition from Equation (20) to graph compatibility. The noninjective compiler is informed by the robustness question behind Problem 5.2. Its class \(\mathsf{Cov}_p(G)\) is a generic-chamber refinement, is definitionally contained in the matched-existential class \(\mathsf{soft2M}_{2,p}(G)\), and is not identified with the published \(\mathrm{soft}_2(G)\); a witnesswise inclusion is asserted only after the source-model admissibility conditions are checked. Squires, Seigal, Bhate, and Uhler (2023) treat injective mixing \(p\ge q\): their generic-soft theorem recovers the transitive closure, while their perfect-intervention clause recovers \(G\); the information-frontier headline here is exclusively noninjective, \(p<q\). Zhang, Greenewald, Squires et al. (2023) treat unpaired observational and interventional data under generalized faithfulness and recover an equivalence class; they neither give nor rule out the noninjective positive-real covariance branch frontier, dense realization covers, separators, or bit-complexity compiler studied here. Sullivant, Talaska, and Draisma (2010) and Foygel, Draisma, and Drton (2012) inform the terminal path-cancellation and max-flow certificate. Foygel Barber et al. (2022) study half-trek criteria for identifiability of latent-variable models; the paper is used only as methodological context and not as an algorithmic or complexity comparator. Sections IV--V of Kela et al. (2020) provide semidefinite tests and positive-semidefinite decomposition and realization machinery for latent causal structures; no dual-separator, positive-real branch-union, or complexity result is attributed to them. In arXiv:2410.23102v1, Boege and Solus (2024), Theorem 3.10, transfer semialgebraic constraints through an affine-birational parametrization with positive localizing denominators, and Theorem 3.11 gives the saturated vanishing ideal. These results inform constraint transfer only: this branch union is not claimed birational, and their paper does not supply its compiler. Wu et al. (2026) use tree dynamic programming to accelerate general existential Fourier--Motzkin elimination and cylindrical algebraic decomposition, with width measured by the primal graph of variables co-occurring in atomic constraints. Covariance-terminal width measures a domain-specific active latent frontier together with a \(p(p+1)/2\)-dimensional moment state. Domination in either direction is unknown without a quantitative translation theorem. The only claimed output distinction is that the compiler returns a dense positive-real realization cover or a full-dimensional separator for graph-frontier membership, whereas generic quantifier elimination or cylindrical algebraic decomposition returns a semialgebraic decision description.
body.technical_internal_limitation: Exact symbolic evidence establishes the actual-row determinant obstruction, a lossless regular reduction of the \(p=2,q=4\) fork to eight bivariate systems, and a rational covariance collision with positive candidate variances \(T+144/121\) and \(19/4\) for every \(T>0\), \(T\ne1\). These checks do not complete the eight-branch chamber classification. The width definition and local sign-decomposition bound must be proved to compose under branch gluing. No quantitative translation between covariance-terminal width and the primal-constraint treewidth of Wu et al. is known, so no comparative complexity claim is made. Only covariance generic loci contain \(\prod_{k\in V}(t_k-v_k)\), so no pointwise variance-neutral conclusion is claimed.
body.honest_scope: Every information-frontier statement is restricted to noninjective mixing \(2\le p<q\); no novelty or equality claim is made for \(p=q\). All graph pairs are DAGs on the same node set, have common transitive closure, and are written in a common topological order. The ambient model includes all \(v_k>0\) and \(t_k>0\), including \(t_k=v_k\). Only theorem-specific covariance loci exclude \(\prod_{k\in V}(t_k-v_k)=0\); both adjacent signs are covered, candidate twins may be variance-neutral, and excluded true hyperplanes receive no pointwise claim. The definitional relation \(\mathsf{Cov}_p(G)\subseteq\mathsf{soft2M}_{2,p}(G)\) is non-headline. Containment in, equality with, or strict inclusion relative to the published covariance-compatible class is outside the claims until every maintained positive-real exact-support witness is checked against the source model. Common permutations are enumerated, nonzero diagonal scales are fixed by the rational projective gauge, and the quotient proposition certifies invariance of all outputs. The mandatory first proof is the full eight-branch fork classification against the original five covariance equations. The bounded-width compiler, including its certificate and bit bound, is next; the all-graph compiler is explicitly open. Terminal-copy compatibility is an independent structural correction. As a sanity reduction, when a branch has a unique positive baseline decomposition and every nonroot loading difference has only one graph-admissible line, the branch system reduces to the terminal affine tests and returns no covariance-only alternative. Recovery of aligned factors from raw laws, finite-sample inference, multitarget interventions, and nonlinear mixing are outside scope.
